planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring; in zone 9 plant February-April. Mammoth is largely self-infertile and needs a genetically distinct cultivar such as Apollo, Coolidge, or Unique planted nearby for good fruit set. Established plants tolerate brief dips to around 15-18F, making them reliable in zone 8 and zone 9. Harvest fruit as it falls naturally October-December.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil; Mammoth is an older New Zealand-selected feijoa cultivar named for its unusually large, elongated fruit, which can weigh well over 4 ounces and sometimes tops the size chart among common home-garden feijoa varieties. The flesh is aromatic and juicy with the classic pineapple-guava-mint flavor, though quality is somewhat more seed-heavy toward the fruit's center than in top dessert cultivars like Apollo. Mammoth ripens mid-to-late season, extending harvest when planted with earlier cultivars, and its vigorous, upright growth habit makes it useful as an informal evergreen screening hedge as well as a fruiting shrub. Because Mammoth sets fruit poorly on its own pollen, interplanting with a second cultivar is essential for a worthwhile crop; the showy white-and-crimson spring flowers and edible sweet petals are ornamental bonuses either way.
sources: California Rare Fruit Growers — Feijoa Cultivar Selection
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Feijoa Production Guide
New Zealand Institute for Plant and Food Research — Feijoa Variety Notes

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring; in zone 9 plant February-April. Triumph is self-infertile and must be planted with a distinct cultivar such as Mammoth or Apollo for cross-pollination and fruit set. Established plants tolerate brief dips to around 15-18F, making them reliable in zone 8 and zone 9. Harvest fruit as it falls naturally October-December.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil; Triumph is a long-established feijoa cultivar, historically one of the standard commercial pollinator partners for Mammoth, producing medium-large, egg-shaped fruit with a thicker skin and firmer, slightly grittier flesh than dessert-focused modern selections. The flavor is good and aromatic though generally ranked a step below top-tier cultivars like Apollo or Unique, making Triumph best grown as a reliable cropping and pollinating partner rather than the star of the planting. It ripens mid-to-late season and stores and ships a bit better than softer-fleshed cultivars because of its firmer texture. The evergreen, silvery-backed foliage and edible spring flowers make it a handsome dual-purpose hedge or specimen shrub regardless of fruit rank.
sources: California Rare Fruit Growers — Feijoa Cultivar Selection
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Feijoa Production Guide
New Zealand Institute for Plant and Food Research — Feijoa Variety Notes

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring; in zone 9 plant February-April. Unique is self-fertile and can crop well on its own, though fruit set and size improve further with a second cultivar such as Apollo or Mammoth nearby. Established plants tolerate brief dips to around 15-18F, making them reliable in zone 8 and zone 9. Harvest fruit as it falls naturally October-December.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil; Unique is a self-fertile New Zealand feijoa cultivar that reliably sets a good crop as a single plant, making it the best choice for gardeners with room for only one bush. Fruits are medium-large, pear-shaped, and smooth-skinned with sweet, aromatic, low-seed flesh and a good balance of pineapple-guava flavor, ripening across a fairly long mid-to-late season window rather than all at once. Because it does not depend on a pollinator partner, Unique is a popular choice for small urban gardens, patios, and hedgerows where only one feijoa can be fit in, though a second cultivar nearby will still increase yield and fruit size. The compact, dense, evergreen habit takes well to hedging or espalier, and the edible spring flowers are a bonus harvest in their own right.
sources: California Rare Fruit Growers — Feijoa Cultivar Selection
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Feijoa Production Guide
New Zealand Institute for Plant and Food Research — Feijoa Variety Notes

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring after frost; Kerman is a female cultivar and needs a male pollinator such as Peters planted within wind-pollination range (one male per 8-10 females is typical) to set nuts.

directions: Kerman is the standard commercial female pistachio cultivar grown across California's Central Valley, chosen for its large nut size and heavy production once mature, though trees can take 7-10 years to bear a full crop. It needs the same demanding climate as the species overall: 700-1000 hours of winter chill combined with long, blisteringly hot, low-humidity summers to fill and split the shells properly, which makes it a poor fit for humid Gulf Coast gardens even where winter cold is adequate. Plant in deep, well-drained, alkaline soil and expect strong biennial bearing, with a heavy crop one year followed by a lighter one the next. A male pollinator such as Peters must bloom at the same time and be planted nearby, since pistachio is wind-pollinated and entirely dioecious. Harvest when hulls loosen and nuts show the characteristic natural shell split, typically in early autumn.
sources: University of California Cooperative Extension — Pistachio Production Manual

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring after frost; Peters is a male, non-fruiting pollinator cultivar planted at a ratio of roughly one tree per 8-10 female Kerman trees, positioned upwind or centrally for reliable wind pollination.

directions: Peters is the standard male pollinator paired with Kerman and other female pistachio cultivars in commercial and home orchards; it produces no nuts itself but times its pollen shed to overlap with Kerman bloom, which is essential since pistachio is entirely wind-pollinated and dioecious. Grow it under the same demanding regime as female pistachio trees: deep, well-drained, alkaline soil, 700-1000 winter chill hours, and hot, dry summers, conditions that make the species a poor match for humid climates regardless of cultivar. In a home planting, a single Peters tree, sited centrally or upwind of the prevailing spring breeze, is usually enough to pollinate several female trees. Because it carries no fruit load, Peters tends to grow a bit more vigorously and can be pruned harder to keep its canopy from overtopping the females it is meant to serve.
sources: University of California Cooperative Extension — Pistachio Production Manual
